items.label: text
items.text: Safety Note: Wear eye protection and heat carefully to avoid cracking the glass syringe with the flame. Take care not to push the opposite plunger completely out!.

items.label: section_header
items.text: KEYPOINT

items.label: text
items.text: When doing this experiment we need to make sure that we use enough copper to react with all the oxygen in the air - the copper must be in excess. There will be some unreacted copper metal at the end. If we do not use enough copper then the value we will get for the percentage of oxygen will be too low because not all of the oxygen will have been removed.

items.label: section_header
items.text: KEYPOINT

items.label: text
items.text: We have put inverted commas around 'air' because we are now talking about air from which the oxygen has been removed, so it is mostly nitrogen. Nitrogen is very unreactive and so if you put a lighted splint into this 'air' it would be extinguished. Oxygen is needed for things to burn.

items.label: section_header
items.text: ACTIVITY 1

items.label: section_header
items.text: PRACTICAL: USING COPPER

items.label: text
items.text: The apparatus shown in Figure 13.2 can be used to find the percentage of oxygen in the air.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Figure 13.2 Using copper to measure the percentage of oxygen in air.

items.label: list_item
items.text: The plunger on one of the gas syringes is pushed all the way in and the other moved out to 100 cm³. We now know that the apparatus contains 100 cm³ air.

items.label: list_item
items.text: The silica tube is heated strongly (roaring Bunsen flame).

items.label: list_item
items.text: The plunger in the left-hand gas syringe is pushed in. This causes the air to pass over the heated copper. This pushes out the plunger on the right-hand gas syringe.

items.label: list_item
items.text: The plungers are pushed in sequence so that the air in the system keeps passing over the heated copper. The pink-brown copper turns black as copper(lI)oxide is formed.

items.label: list_item
items.text: As the copper reacts, the Bunsen burner is moved along the tube so that it is always heatingfresh copper.

items.label: list_item
items.text: The volume of gas in the syringes falls as the oxygen is consumed.

items.label: list_item
items.text: We keep pushing the plungers in and out until there is no change in volume.

items.label: list_item
items.text: The apparatus is then allowed to cool to room temperature again before taking the final volume of gas (because gases expand as they are heated).

items.label: section_header
items.text: RESULTS

items.label: table
items.text:
| initial volume of air In the system/cm³   |   100 |
|-------------------------------------------|-------|
| final volume of 'air' in the system/cm³   |    79 |

items.label: text
items.text: The volume of the air has decreased because the oxygen has been removed as it reacts with the copper. The reaction that occurs is

items.label: formula
items.text: 2 C u ( s ) + \ O _ { 2 } ( g ) \, \rightarrow \, \ 2 C u O ( s )

items.label: text
items.text: copper + oxygen → copper(Ill) oxide

items.label: text
items.text: We can work out from these data that the volume of oxygen that reacted was 100-79 = 21 cm³.

items.label: text
items.text: The original volume of air was100 cm³ so we can work out the percentage of oxygen in the air:

items.label: text
items.text: percentage oxygen = 21/100 × 100 = 21%
